title: Noise Complaints
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien, a learning specialist for inclusion, reflects on what worked in 2025 and names accessible design as the biggest win. Drawing on a Steplab paper, he frames extraneous load as noise and argues that making resources accessible by default shifted inclusion from an additive burden on some teachers into a whole-school professional development focus. He admits he once over-decorated slides with colour, animation and gifs, which only added stimuli competing for working memory. His prescription is dyslexic-friendly sans-serif fonts, dark text on pale backgrounds, animations that reveal information as it becomes relevant, images on their own slides, and information left visible while needed. He ends by clarifying that the aim is to optimise rather than minimise cognitive load, since too little difficulty reduces motivation.
points: Accessible design gave inclusion a whole-school angle because it makes every lesson inclusive by default instead of adding work for teachers of students with additional needs.
Colourful, animated slides add stimuli that compete with the learning, so Brien cuts instructional noise under the K.I.S.S. principle.
Concrete rules include sans-serif fonts, high contrast, revealing information as it becomes relevant, and keeping needed information on screen.
Teachers save time by not hunting for gifs and can spend it on embedding checks for understanding.
The goal is optimal, not minimal, cognitive load, because easy material loses motivation.
quotes: As teacher’s we know that students have a limited working memory and the more novel stimuli they are subjected too the more likely it is they will face cognitive overload and will struggle to transfer relevant information to long term memory.

I’m guilty in the past of doing too much with my resources. I thought that if I made them colourful and animated as well as including images and gifs that I would be able to keep students engaged. In reality, this just creates more and more stimuli for the students to discern between and creates additional noise to prevent the important learning breaking through.

All of our teaching resources should be accessible to all students by default. This means that all resources should aim to be in a dyslexic friendly sans-serif font such as arial, aptos, calibri or opendyslexic. There should be dark text on pale backgrounds for high contrast, and extraneous load should be minimized where possible.
Information should also remain visible while it is relevant otherwise it must be stored in working memory and therefore continues to add on to cognitive load.

Our focus on accessible design this year has meant that teachers can actually save time when creating new resources as they do not need to trawl the internet for hours for the perfect gif of a dog skateboarding. Instead they have been able to spend that time creating and embedding meaningful checks for understanding throughout their lessons so that we know if learning is taking place during that lesson.

One final note on all of this. In cutting the instructional noise we are not aiming to minimise cognitive load for students. At all times we are aiming to optimise cognitive load. If cognitive load is minimised students may actually find the learning to easy and therefore load motivation while optimising the load leads to those desirable levels of difficulty where strong learning can occur.
